content: Febrile seizures can be categorized into two types: simple febrile seizures and complex febrile seizures. Complex febrile seizures are characterized by episodes associated with fever that persist for more than 15 minutes, occur more than once within a 24-hour period, and are localized to one side of the child’s body. In certain countries, it is a common practice for physicians to recommend an electroencephalograph (EEG) for children who experience complex febrile seizures. However, there is limited evidence available to support the utility of EEG or to determine the optimal timing for its use in this context. The objective of this review was to evaluate the role of EEG and its timing in children under the age of five who have experienced complex febrile seizures. For the most recent update of this review, a comprehensive search was conducted on March 12, 2019, across several databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), which encompasses the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), as well as MEDLINE (Ovid, 1946 to March 11, 2019) and ClinicalTrials.gov. No restrictions were applied regarding the language of the studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the utility of EEG and its timing following complex febrile seizures in children. Articles were selected and reviewed independently by the authors, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consultation with the Cochrane Epilepsy Group. Standard methodological procedures as outlined by Cochrane were followed throughout the review process. Out of 48 studies that were initially identified as potentially eligible, none of the studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. Consequently, no RCTs were found to provide evidence either supporting or refuting the use of EEG or its timing in children under five years of age who have experienced complex febrile seizures. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence from RCTs to guide the use of EEG or its timing in this population. They suggested that a randomized controlled trial could be designed in which participants are randomly assigned to either an EEG group or a non-EEG group, with an adequately powered sample size to address this question. Since the last version of this review, no new studies have been identified.
